'''Paolo Sassone-Corsi''' (8 June 1956 – 22 July 2020) was an Italian [[Molecular Biologist|molecular biologist]], [[Epigenetics|epigeneticist]], and [[research]]er. He is known for his contributions in the areas of [[transcriptional regulation]], [[epigenetics]], [[Circadian rhythm|circadian]] biology, and [[Metabolism|metabolic]] regulation.<ref name=":0" /> He is known for his contributions in the areas of [[transcriptional regulation]], [[epigenetics]], circadian biology, and [[Metabolism|metabolic]] regulation. His research primarily focused on the mechanisms that regulate transcription and their relation to [[metabolism]] and [[circadian clock]]s. His work focused on understanding how the [[circadian clock]] regulates [[Metabolism|metabolic]] cycles. Most notably, he discovered that [[Sirtuin 1|SIRT1]], a [[histone deacetylase]] with a critical role in [[gene expression]] and [[metabolism]], is able to regulate the activity of the [[CLOCK]] protein.<ref name=":4" /> In 2011, Sassone-Corsi founded and directed the “Center for Epigenetics and Metabolism” at the [[University of California, Irvine]].

==Biography==
Paolo Sassone-Corsi was born in Naples, Italy on June 8, 1956.<ref name=":3" /> He devoted himself to science and soccer at an early age.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Masri |first1=Selma |last2=Goding |first2=Colin R. |last3=Leff |first3=Todd |date=17 September 2020 |title=Paolo Sassone-Corsi (1956–2020) |journal=Cell |volume=182 |issue=6 |pages=1363–1365 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.019 |s2cid=221766547 |issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free }}</ref> Together with his brother Emilio Sassone-Corsi, they founded the Neapolitan Astronomy Club (Gruppo Astrofili Napoletani)<ref name=":5" /> and eventually published a paper on the bands of Saturn. Their works were awarded the Philips Prize for Young Researchers. They worked at the Paris Meudon Observatory where they studied Saturn.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Bifulco |first1=Maurizio |last2=Usiello |first2=Alessandro |date=2020-09-15 |title=Remembering Paolo Sassone-Corsi |journal=Cell Death & Disease |language=en |volume=11 |issue=9 |pages=759 |doi=10.1038/s41419-020-02975-z |issn=2041-4889 |pmc=7493942 |pmid=32934198}}</ref> His passions grew from astronomy to biology, and eventually genetics.<ref name=":5" />

Sassone-Corsi completed his graduate studies on yeast biology and graduated with a doctorate in biological science from the [[University of Naples Federico II]] in 1979.<ref name=":0" /> Following this, Sassone-Corsi moved to [[Strasbourg]] and went on to complete a post-doctoral fellowship under the instruction of [[Pierre Chambon]] at the Institut de Génétique et de Biologie Moléculaire et Cellulaire (IGBMC) in Strasbourg, France. During his time under Chambon, Sassone-Corsi was drawn to transcription mechanisms and contributed to key work on promoters, enhancers and transactivating factors.<ref name=":0" />

In search of innovation, he and his wife moved to [[San Diego]], United States where he worked as a post-doctoral fellow under [[Inder Verma]] at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]] from 1986 to 1989. At the Salk Institute, most of his work was focused on the study of the intracellular pathway that leads to the activation of proto-oncogenes c-''fos'' and c-''jun.''<ref name=":0" />

In 1989, he began working as a research director for the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] at [[:fr:Institut de génétique et de biologie moléculaire et cellulaire|Institut de Génétique et de Biologie Moléculaire et Cellulaire]] (IGBMC) in Strasbourg, France. He started his own independent laboratory at IGBMC and progressed to the director of research at the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique.  During his time here, Sassone-Corsi identified and characterized the role of the [[CAMP responsive element modulator|cAMP-responsive element modulator (CREM)]] in spermatogenesis.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sassone-Corsi |first=Paolo |date=2002-06-21 |title=Unique Chromatin Remodeling and Transcriptional Regulation in Spermatogenesis |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1070963 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=296 |issue=5576 |pages=2176–2178 |doi=10.1126/science.1070963 |pmid=12077401 |bibcode=2002Sci...296.2176S |s2cid=9713089 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Beginning in 2006, he worked for the [[University of California, Irvine]] as a professor and head of chair of the pharmacology department.  In 2011, he founded and directed the Center of Epigenetics and Metabolism.<ref name=":3">{{cite web |title=Paolo Sassone-Corsi |url=https://www.faculty.uci.edu/profile.cfm?faculty_id=5402 |work=UC Irvine}}</ref> 

During the course of his life, Sassone-Corsi has published multiple books. In 2013, he published a book of reflections titled "Ti sembra il Caso?: Schermaglia fra un narratore e un biologo", written alongside [[Erri De Luca]].<ref name="La Repubblica">{{cite web|url=https://www.repubblica.it/rubriche/passaparola/2013/04/08/news/erri_de_luca-56206838/|title=Uno scrittore e un biologo: schermaglia su Dna e Caso|date=8 April 2013|work=La Repubblica|language=Italian}}</ref> He also wrote another book with [[Erri De Luca]]<ref name="La Repubblica"/> in 2016 about the intersections of biology, music and poetry.

==Scientific contributions==
Sassone-Corsi's work largely focused on the implementation of molecular approaches for [[cell signaling]], [[circadian rhythm]], [[epigenetics]], and the plasticity of the genome.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.inserm.fr/actualites-et-evenements/actualites/premier-atlas-metabolisme-circadien|title=Un premier atlas du métabolisme circadien|date=9 October 2018|work=Inserm|language=French}}</ref> Through the study of signal transduction mechanisms, he investigated how they modulate nuclear functions such as gene expression, chromatin remodeling, and epigenetic control.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Verdin |first=Eric |date=2020-10-30 |title=Paolo Sassone-Corsi (1956–2020) |journal=Science |language=en |volume=370 |issue=6516 |pages=532 |doi=10.1126/science.abe9149 |pmid=33122373 |s2cid=225965236 |issn=0036-8075|doi-access=free }}</ref>

'''Early research on transcription'''

During his time as a postdoc, working under the mentorship of [[Pierre Chambon]] at IGBCM in 1980, Sassone-Corsi studied transcriptional elements and identified the promoter sequence of the adenovirus major late gene, which later became known as the [[TATA box]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Masri |first1=Selma |last2=Nakahata |first2=Yasukazu |last3=Eckel-Mahan |first3=Kristin |date=December 2020 |title=Paolo Sassone-Corsi |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0748730420962657 |journal=Journal of Biological Rhythms |language=en |volume=35 |issue=6 |pages=515–518 |doi=10.1177/0748730420962657 |s2cid=222217275 |issn=0748-7304|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Later, Sassone-Corsi moved to the Salk Institute for Biological Studies and made important advancements in understanding the transcriptional autoregulation of the proto-oncogene, ''fos''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Sassone-Corsi |first1=Paolo |last2=Sisson |first2=John C. |last3=Verma |first3=Inder M. |date=July 1988 |title=Transcriptional autoregulation of the proto-oncogene fos |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/334314a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=334 |issue=6180 |pages=314–319 |doi=10.1038/334314a0 |pmid=2839774 |bibcode=1988Natur.334..314S |s2cid=4337642 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Oncogenes which encode for nuclear proteins include, ''fos, jun,'' and ''p53'', just to name a few.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Ransone |first1=L. J. |last2=Verma |first2=I. M. |date=1989-06-01 |title=Association of nuclear oncoproteins fos and jun |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0955-0674%2889%2990017-3 |journal=Current Opinion in Cell Biology |language=en |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=536–540 |doi=10.1016/0955-0674(89)90017-3 |pmid=2516738 |issn=0955-0674|url-access=subscription }}</ref> As a nuclear oncogene, ''fos'' is able to initiate cell growth, differentiation, and development which can cause cancer if over-induced. The c-fos protein contains a "[[leucine zipper]]" that allows it to form a heterodimer with ''jun'', another oncogene.<ref name=":6" /> In 1988, Sassone-Corsi found that proto-oncogenes [[Protein c-Fos|''c-fos'']] and [[Transcription factor Jun|''c-jun'']] are activated through a pathway which regulates transcription; ''c-fos'' and ''c-jun'' interact with each other to form a homodimer, [[AP-1 transcription factor|AP-1]], and that ''c-fos'' is regulated by [[Cyclic adenosine monophosphate|cAMP]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> AP-1 is much more stable than either the ''fos'' or ''jun'' homodimer and can bind to the necessary promoter sequences much more effectively.<ref name=":6" /> As such, AP-1 has a significant role in the cell cycle.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Angel |first1=P. |last2=Karin |first2=M. |date=1991-12-10 |title=The role of Jun, Fos and the AP-1 complex in cell-proliferation and transformation |journal=Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer |volume=1072 |issue=2–3 |pages=129–157 |doi=10.1016/0304-419x(91)90011-9 |issn=0006-3002 |pmid=1751545}}</ref>

'''Circadian biology research'''

In 2006, Sassoni-Corsi illuminated the role of [[chromatin remodeling]] in circadian mechanisms through the discovery that [[CLOCK]] acts as a [[Histone acetyltransferase|histone acetyltransferase (HAT)]] by recruiting [[EP300|P300]] and CBP, allowing it to help restore rhythmicity in ''Clock'' mutants. This activity allows CLOCK to control the acetylation of [[ARNTL|BMAL1]] and [[Histone H3|H3]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Doi |first1=Masao |last2=Hirayama |first2=Jun |last3=Sassone-Corsi |first3=Paolo |date=2006-05-05 |title=Circadian Regulator CLOCK Is a Histone Acetyltransferase |journal=Cell |language=en |volume=125 |issue=3 |pages=497–508 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2006.03.033 |pmid=16678094 |s2cid=5968161 |issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free }}</ref> This was important in demonstrating the role of chromatin remodeling in the core clock mechanism and revealed new associations between cellular physiology and histone acetylation. He later helped discover that the [[Histone deacetylase|histone deacetylase (HDAC)]] activity of [[Sirtuin 1|SIRT1]], which is [[Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide|NAD+]] dependent, undergoes circadian regulation, counteracts the HAT activity of CLOCK, and has ''in vivo'' circadian control.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nakahata |first1=Yasukazu |last2=Kaluzova |first2=Milota |last3=Grimaldi |first3=Benedetto |last4=Sahar |first4=Saurabh |last5=Hirayama |first5=Jun |last6=Chen |first6=Danica |last7=Guarente |first7=Leonard P. |last8=Sassone-Corsi |first8=Paolo |date=2008-07-25 |title=The NAD+-Dependent Deacetylase SIRT1 Modulates CLOCK-Mediated Chromatin Remodeling and Circadian Control |journal=Cell |language=en |volume=134 |issue=2 |pages=329–340 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2008.07.002 |pmid=18662547 |pmc=3526943 |issn=0092-8674}}</ref> In 2009, Sassone-Corsi also helped discover that [[Nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase|NAMPT]], a rate-limiting step involved in NAD+ salvaging, has circadian expression regulated by CLOCK:BMAL1. His research found that NAMPT was essential to altering the circadian expression of genes; in the same study, he discovered a transcriptional-enzymatic feedback loop between circadian rhythms and cellular metabolism which was an impactful contribution to investigating the links between the two.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Nakahata |first1=Yasukazu |last2=Sahar |first2=Saurabh |last3=Astarita |first3=Giuseppe |last4=Kaluzova |first4=Milota |last5=Sassone-Corsi |first5=Paolo |date=May 2009 |title=Circadian Control of the NAD + Salvage Pathway by CLOCK-SIRT1 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=324 |issue=5927 |pages=654–657 |doi=10.1126/science.1170803 |issn=0036-8075 |pmc=6501775 |pmid=19286518|bibcode=2009Sci...324..654N }}</ref>

'''Signaling pathways'''

Sassone-Corsi was influential in investigating the role of [[chromatin]] in signaling with a study he conducted in 2000. He revealed that signaling pathways act directly on chromatin components to regulate certain processes; N-terminal tails of histones are acted upon with reversible covalent modifications to elicit responses in multiple pathways.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Cheung |first1=Peter |last2=Allis |first2=C.David |last3=Sassone-Corsi |first3=Paolo |date=13 October 2000 |title=Signaling to Chromatin through Histone Modifications |journal=Cell |volume=103 |issue=2 |pages=263–271 |doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(00)00118-5 |pmid=11057899 |s2cid=16237908 |issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free }}</ref> They investigated the interactions that occur when multiple modifications are present on the N-terminal tails at the same time and proposed that H2B-H3 and H2A-H4 are the tails which act as signaling platforms. His research segued into a broader understanding of the role histone modifications play in the complex circuitries of gene regulation.<ref name=":2" />

Sassone-Corsi looked further into the coupling of histone modifications and found evidence of synergistic coupling of H3 phosphorylation and acetylation in response to [[epidermal growth factor]] stimulation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cheung |first1=Peter |last2=Tanner |first2=Kirk G |last3=Cheung |first3=Wang L |last4=Sassone-Corsi |first4=Paolo |last5=Denu |first5=John M |last6=Allis |first6=C.David |date=1 June 2000 |title=Synergistic Coupling of Histone H3 Phosphorylation and Acetylation in Response to Epidermal Growth Factor Stimulation |journal=Molecular Cell |volume=5 |issue=6 |pages=905–915 |doi=10.1016/s1097-2765(00)80256-7 |pmid=10911985 |issn=1097-2765|doi-access=free }}</ref> He identified that EGF stimulation activates the [[MAPK/ERK pathway|MAP kinase]] pathway which leads to sequential modifications of chromatin.
